links.note: Around 600 the Georgian church, led by its catholicos Kurion, accepted the Council of Chalcedon. The Armenian catholicos Abraham condemned him at a council in Dvin. Samuel of Ani, a twelfth-century Armenian chronicler, records that the Georgians separated after adopting Chalcedon. Scholars date the break anywhere from 596 to 609.

prose_changes.old: The kingdom of Kartli, in what is now eastern Georgia, became Christian in the fourth century through the preaching of a woman the tradition calls Nino, and then spent three centuries holding that identity on a frontier where Persia had every reason to prise it loose. Its oldest surviving book, written in the 470s or 480s, is the account of Shushanik. An Armenian princess married to the local ruler, who abandoned Christianity for Zoroastrianism and imprisoned and beat his wife until she died rather than follow him. Georgia developed its own alphabet, its own monasteries, and an unusually rich liturgical life: Georgian manuscripts preserve the worship of fifth- to eighth-century Jerusalem more fully than any Greek source does. In 609, at the third council of Dvin, its church broke with Armenia and took the Chalcedonian side. Which is why the two neighboring Caucasian churches have belonged to different communions ever since.

prose_changes.old: The Georgian Orthodox Church that emerged is still the church of Georgia, and the same institution continued through the medieval revival centuries into the present. Its choice in 609 placed it permanently in the Eastern Orthodox family rather than with its Armenian neighbor. Its greatest bequest to everyone else is almost accidental. Because Georgian scribes translated and kept Jerusalem's liturgical books, scholars can now reconstruct how the holy city actually worshipped in late antiquity largely from Georgian manuscripts. And churches built at the very end of this period, like Jvari above Mtskheta, are still standing almost unaltered.

prose_changes.old: Beside Armenia and Georgia there was a third Christian kingdom in the Caucasus. Albania, in what is now Azerbaijan and southern Dagestan, with its own royal line, its own bishops and its own alphabet. It held a council at Aghuen in the late fifth century that issued canons on clergy, marriage and what the nobility owed the church, and it produced a history — compiled from earlier material by a writer known as Movses Daskhurantsi. That is very nearly all the narrative it left. Pressed between Persian, Byzantine and then Arab power, and between the competing alignments of its Armenian and Georgian neighbors, it lost its independent standing in 705, when its catholicosate was placed under the Armenian church. Its written language was effectively lost for more than a thousand years, until palimpsests found at Saint Catherine's Monastery on Sinai in 1996 turned out to preserve Caucasian Albanian scripture beneath later Georgian text.

prose_changes.old: No church continues under this name — after 705 its structures were absorbed into the Armenian catholicosate and its separate identity dissolved into its neighbors'. The Udi people of Azerbaijan are generally regarded as descendants of its Christian population. Its most striking survival was invisible until recently: the palimpsests recovered at Sinai in 1996 preserved its alphabet and its scripture, letting scholars begin to reconstruct a language and a liturgy that nobody had been able to read for over a millennium.
prose_changes.new: No church continues under this name. After 705 its catholicos came under the authority of the Armenian church. The see itself lived on inside that church, and a new catholicos of Albania was installed around 1701. Over the centuries its people merged with the Armenians, and the see was abolished early in the nineteenth century. The Udi people of Azerbaijan are generally regarded as descendants of its Christian population. Its most striking survival was invisible until recently: in 1996 palimpsests at Sinai were found to preserve its alphabet and its scripture. They let scholars begin to reconstruct a language and a liturgy that nobody had been able to read for over a millennium.
prose_changes.reason: The old text said its structures were 'absorbed' after 705 and its identity 'dissolved'. Vendored sources show the see lasted: Hasan-Jalaliants was installed as the 92nd catholicos of Aghovanie in 1701/2 and given investiture by the Armenian catholicos (Brosset 1876, lines 10702-10708); Ormanian (p. 132, lines 6147-6155) says the see was abolished early in the nineteenth century 'on account of the fusion of the Caspio-Albanian or Aghouanian nationality with the Armenian'. The palimpsest wording as above.
